# Cut the AI tells, keep the voice

Peter Yang · Evaluation · `ai-slop-edit`

Peter Yang’s no-ai-slop skill names the patterns that make writing sound machine-made: empty superlatives, false contrasts, throat-clearing openers and closing lines that try to sound profound. Make the minimum effective edit: cut the patterns, keep the facts and leave the writer’s own voice intact.

**Use when:** When an AI draft sounds like everyone else’s, when it’s full of words like seamless and cutting-edge, or when you want to check a piece before it’s published.

**Keep in mind:** When the goal is to fool an AI detector. These patterns say nothing about who wrote a piece, and a rough sentence with a real voice should stay.

## Principles

- Make the minimum effective edit. Remove the patterns, errors and repetition but keep strong sentences, humor, hesitation and quirks. The piece should still sound like the same person afterward.
- Run the portability test. If a sentence could move unchanged to another company, country or product, it’s probably filler. Cut it or replace it with a fact, example or consequence that only applies here.
- Cut the constructions: “It’s not X, it’s Y” (just say Y), throat-clearing openers like “Here’s the thing” and “Let’s dive in,” colon reveals like “The best part: …,” clusters of em dashes, recap endings and closing lines that try to sound deep.
- Swap empty words for what they should mean. Seamless, robust, leverage, delve, unlock your potential and in today’s fast-paced world say nothing on their own – write what the product does, for whom and how.
- Show rather than tell the reader what to think. Cut “this matters” and “the interesting part is” and let facts, examples and consequences carry the point.
- Name the source or cut the claim. “Experts agree” and “studies show” without a source should go; ask for the evidence rather than inventing it.

## Choose a move for the situation

- The text is full of adjectives: An empty word becomes a fact and A triplet for the rhythm.
- The text never gets to the point: Throat-clearing and False contrast.
- The ending sounds like a lecture: A closing line that tries to sound profound.
- You are unsure whether a sentence is filler: The portability test.

## Moves

- **An empty word becomes a fact.** Ask what the word would mean if it were true, and write that. “A seamless experience” becomes “You sign in with your fingerprint and you’re done.”
- **False contrast.** Cut what nobody claimed and state the second half directly. “It’s not about technology, it’s about people” becomes “We train the staff before the system goes live.”
- **Throat-clearing.** Cut the opener and start with the sentence that follows it. “Here’s the thing: most forms are too long” becomes “Most forms are too long.”
- **A triplet for the rhythm.** Three adjectives in a row are often there because they sound good. Keep what you can back up. “Fast, simple and secure” becomes “Done in two minutes.”
- **A closing line that tries to sound profound.** Cut it and end on the last concrete fact or on the next step. “Because at the end of the day, it’s about trust.” Cut it. The last line becomes “Book a walkthrough.”
- **The portability test.** Would the sentence fit unchanged at a competitor? Then it says nothing about you. “We’re passionate about our customers” could run anywhere. “We reply to email within one business day” can only run where it is true.

## Questions to ask

- Which sentences would work just as well for a competitor?
- What in the piece sounds like the writer, and how do we protect it?
- Which claims lack a named source or a concrete fact?

## Fictional example

Fictional: Ledger & Co. handles day-to-day bookkeeping for small businesses, and every client gets a dedicated contact to email.

- **Before:** In today’s fast-paced world, it’s not just about bookkeeping – it’s about freedom. Ledger & Co. offers a seamless, tailored solution that unlocks your potential.
- **After:** Ledger & Co. handles your day-to-day bookkeeping, and you get a dedicated contact to email whenever something is unclear.
- **Why:** The buzzwords and the false contrast are gone; what remains is what the service does and who the reader can ask.

## A complete example

Fictional: a LinkedIn post by the founder of Ledger & Co., a bookkeeping firm. Facts in the brief: the firm has started replying to client emails within one business day, and every client now has a named contact with a direct line. The writer usually writes short and a little dry.

**Draft:**

> In today’s fast-paced world, bookkeeping is not just about numbers. It’s about trust. Here’s the thing: most firms see you as an account number. At Ledger & Co. we’ve taken the client experience to the next level with a seamless, personal and tailored service. The best part: you never have to wait. Because at the end of the day, it’s the relationship that counts. 🚀

**Revised:**

> We changed two things at Ledger & Co.
>
> You get a reply to your email within one business day.
>
> You have your own contact, with a name and a direct line. The same person every time.
>
> We should have done it sooner.

**What the example does:**

- Six patterns are gone: empty words, a false contrast, throat-clearing, a colon reveal, a profound closing line and an emoji.
- What remains are the two facts. Nothing was added that wasn’t in the brief.
- The last line is the writer’s own dry tone. It wasn’t in the draft, so the writer should approve it.

## Common mistakes

- Swapping one empty word for another. “Smooth” instead of “seamless” says just as little.
- Sanding away everything that stands out. An awkward sentence with a voice of its own should stay.
- Believing the text is good because the check finds nothing. It finds known phrases, not empty thoughts.
